images.filename: 'Y Waliau' or Slate Dressing area of Sied Australia - geograph.org.uk - 286291.jpg
images.caption:
'Y Waliau' or Slate Dressing area of Sied Australia. Right up to the closure of the quarry in 1969, the slate dressing process at Australia was totally unmechanised. In some other parts of the quarry, dressing machines were used to trim the slates into their final size and squareness. Dressing was a complex process which involved (a) splitting the sawn blocks along the cleavage lines into thin sheets, (b) marking the slate shape with a nail tipped measuring stick, and (c) using a knife to cut the slate to shape. Rotary dressing machines for shaping and squaring were introduced into 6 of Dinorwig's 14 sheds - 170 machines in all. The working area of each team of 4 or 6 men (half of whose members worked on the rock face producing rock for the other half to dress) was demarcated by the horizontal slate slabs.

images.caption: A1 Drum-House. This was the lowest drum house on this 9 pitched incline which bought finished slate products down from the western half of the Dinorwig Quarry to Gilfach Ddu where the trucks were loaded, four at a time, on each of the larger trucks of the Padarn Railway. This drum house had by its side a brakeman's cabin which had its own home comforts including, in winter, a blazing fire. The brakeman's job was to control the descent of the trucks on his particular pitch. 285354

images.caption:
A2 Drum-House This view is taken from the marshalling area behind the A2 drum-house. The steps on the right lead to the Zig-Zag path which links Dinorwig and Llanberis and which was designed to provide handy access to various parts of the western half of the quarry for workers from both villages. The path crosses the tramways by means of the bridge immediately behind the drum-house. The large sheets of slate in the foreground provided shelter for the marshalling area workers.

images.caption: A Lefal at Lernion. A 'lefal' is a slate quarryman's term for an access tunnel into the extraction area. During the construction of the HEP station, this lefal was abandoned and a cutting made to allow access to the gallery for the large machinery needed to create a tunnel access from the gallery to the HEP shaft. The building in Ponc Aberdaron above is a 'cwt mochal ffiar' - a blast shelter. 292261

images.caption: Barics Aberdaron Barracks. These, at 2,100, were the highest barracks at Dinorwig Quarry. On a fine summer's evening, the view from here is fantastic and one can imagine the quarrymen, who stayed here from Monday to Friday nights inclusive, sitting outside conversing, smoking their pipes and looking down towards their homes in Western Anglesey. Likewise, one can try and imagine what it was like in the depth of winter. Heating for barracks throughout the quarry was provided by coal fires and the coal had to bought from the company and sent up from Gilfach Ddu at the very bottom of the quarry. In the mid 1920s, as the Quarry's 'Llyfr Cownt Glo'(Coal Account Book) shows, coal was 2s 2d a hundredweight. Each barrack used about 56lbs a week. Because of the increasing reluctance of men to opt for Aberdaron, the company decided to provide free coal for the barracks and to provide an armchair for each man. The rent at Aberdaron in 1925 was only 1s a month. However, there was no piped water and the men depended on a mountain spring for water to drink, cook and to wash in. 292242

images.filename: Blast Shelter at Ponc Aberdaron - geograph.org.uk - 292261.jpg
images.caption: Blast Shelter at Ponc Aberdaron. This is a large well constructed blast shelter and is the only one on this gallery. A shelter of this size could hold around 36 men. The height of the rockface here is 68 feet.The gallery immediately above is Ponc Llangristiolus, so called because it was first developed by a team led by Owen Rowlands of the parish of Llangristiolus in Anglesey.

images.caption: C6 'Tanc' Incline. The two 'tanc' or 'trwnc' inclines C6, linking Ponc Aifft and Ponc Australia, and C7, linking Ponc Twllmwg and Ponc Aifft, are unique. Here, unlike other inclines where the drum is located in a drum house, the drum is positioned below the trackway bed and is operated from a cabin (the chimney of that of C6 is visible in this photo at the top of the incline) using a device similar to that of a ship's wheel.

images.filename: A Blondin Tower on Ponc Roller Braich - geograph.org.uk - 302083.jpg
images.caption:
A Blondin Tower on Ponc Roller Braich Ponc Roller Braich now ends rather abruptly and as the 'sinc' deepened a Blondin was used to lift and lower wagons to the Roller level. These were railed to and from the foot of the Blondin tower along a tramway laid on a causeway of slate rubble. Lack of maintenance since the quarry closed weakened the causeway leading to a partial collapse. This left part of the railway spanning good mountain air. Charles Blondin might have enjoyed walking across it, but it's certainly a no no unless you happen to have been born with a pair of wings.
302110

images.caption: After the Climb. Many of the climbs in the quarry end at bolts from which the climber is lowered back to terra firma. This is a fantastic slab just of the main 'road' through the quarry. Climbing on slate is very hard as the rock is very smooth and the holds on this climb are very small.
